extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Idler / general educated 18th-century public
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis/extraction of evaluative claims and prescriptive observations found in 18th‑century periodical essays (Samuel Johnson's The Idler). Focuses on the essays' standards for behaviour, judgement, and social practice as expressed in the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate_determinism_is_false
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of government and national character are not the necessary or direct result of climate; civil institutions are seldom the outcome of deliberate reasoning but arise by chance, conquest, or local agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues against those "who derive the civil institutions of every country from its climate," noting that forms of government are often framed by chance, despotism, or occasional laws made by a few. It observes that "national customs can arise only from general agreement" and gives the English notice of the weather as a custom produced by variable skies rather than a cause of national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do_not_enslave_mood_to_weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should not resign their tranquillity and benevolence to the influence of weather; blaming clouds or winds for cheerfulness or peevishness is a moral failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text calls it "the cowardice of idleness, and the idolatry of folly" to "call upon the sun for peace and gaiety, or deprecate the clouds lest sorrow should overwhelm us." It recommends temperance and resolute exertion of faculties so that one may be "superior to the seasons" and not make virtue depend on external meteorological conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance_and_constancy_over_seasonal_excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower degrees of Stoic constancy — resisting impulses from success or calamity and not yielding to seasonal or external excuses — are necessary for common virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While full Stoic invulnerability is unattainable, the essay recommends struggling "against the tyranny of the climate" and cultivating enough steadiness that one is not "enslaved" by changes of weather; daily temperance renders every day propitious to diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity_of_public_names_and_pursuit_of_fame
rubrics_metrics.description: The desire for a name or public distinction is widespread but rarely realized; a name is a "free gift of mankind" that must be deserved and is grudgingly given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay describes the human longing for visible distinction, the special prominence of such desire around marriage announcements, and how the pursuit of a name often leads to vain or temporary satisfactions. It notes that very few can acquire a lasting name, and that the unwillingness of the public to bestow fame increases the individual's desire for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage_panegyrics_are_often_hollow_and_saleable
rubrics_metrics.description: The habitual public praises attached to weddings are frequently formulaic and inessential; such praises can be commodified and are of dubious value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the anecdote of Mr. Settle who maintained a standing elegy/epithalamium adaptable to many occasions and made a livelihood selling panegyrics, the essay suggests that wedding encomiums chiefly gratify vanity and could be omitted without loss to the community. It criticizes the custom as self‑flattering and occasionally mercenary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate_education_for_girls_over_mere_needlework
rubrics_metrics.description: Confining girls to continuous needlework and household crafts at the expense of basic literacy, arithmetic, and general knowledge is a serious educational deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through the narrator's complaint about his wife's insistence on constant needlework for their daughters, the essay gives examples: a daughter who thinks Ireland is in France, another who cannot read a Bible chapter, and one ignorant of Protestant vs. Papist distinctions because she has been embroidering scenes. The critique recommends reading, writing, and arithmetic rather than exclusively domestic handicrafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard_time_against_social_usurpers
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is the most precious property and should be protected; unwanted visits, idle petitioners, and social distractions that seize another's time commit an irreparable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts "time once passed never returns" and catalogs kinds of time‑usurpers: loiterers, consulters who never take advice, boasters, complainers, projectors, economists, politicians, usurers, and perfunctory talkers. He calls attention to the moral wrong of imposing undesired conversation or attendance on others and recommends reflection to prevent such invasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social_kindness_requires_enduring_follies
rubrics_metrics.description: If one desires the kindness and company of others, one must tolerate a measure of their follies and accept the time cost of social interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay counsels that those who seek the convenience of society must sometimes "pay a tribute of his time" to those who are foolish or tiresome: attendance, appearing interested in trivial talk, and accepting interruptions are part of social life and its reciprocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique_of_trifling_speculation_and_pretended_industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Much amateur or superficial inquiry (counting spiders' eyes, repeating trivial experiments) is vain show rather than genuine advancement and often disguises idleness as industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay mocks those who pretend to scientific labour by trivial pursuits: counting eyes with microscopes, separating marigold dust, repeating simple mixtures, or demonstrating obvious phenomena repeatedly. Such activities are presented as harmless if innocent, but often merely display vanity and not true usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation_of_cruel_vivisection_and_unjustified_experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Anatomical cruelty and experiments that mutilate living animals for ostentation or idle curiosity are morally abhorrent and produce little real knowledge to justify their means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author strongly condemns a "race of wretches" among inferior medical practitioners who nail dogs to tables, perform living dissections, and otherwise torture animals. He doubts that these acts have yielded cures or important discoveries and argues they harden the heart and prepare practitioners to be cruel to humans as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public_critique_exposes_the_critic_to_reciprocal_scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: One who seeks distinction through ridicule or censure will likely provoke similar scrutiny and criticism directed back at himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening of No. 18 warns that those who obtain applause by censuring others teach others to practise the same arts against them; the natural discontent of inferiors will operate as malice and subject the critic to examination and exaggeration of faults.
